name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,177

solutions.check: 32 entries, 60 crossings, 0 conflicts, agrees with the 31 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Sinner primarily isn't commonly taken to be such

definitions.text: Sinner primarily isn't commonly taken to be such

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of the word before it is wanted

blocks.note: the first letter of sinner
ain't is the common, non-standard way to say isn't

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer who is, against all expectation, popularly regarded as holy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: 1 4 is SAINT AUGUSTINE, whose Confessions tell of a sinful youth before he became a saint. 'Such' points back to the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A saint is a person recognised as holy, and Augustine is the classic reformed sinner who came to be regarded that way.

clue.text: "— him, and he is no fool. But let him loose among his fellows, and he is lost" (Max Beerbohm, Zuleika Dobson)

definitions.text: "— him, and he is no fool. But let him loose among his fellows, and he is lost" (Max Beerbohm, Zuleika Dobson)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation from Beerbohm's 1911 satire of Oxford
setter's reading: the dash is a blank for the verb meaning set apart from the others

explanation.walkthrough: The verb is the opposite of 'let him loose among his fellows' later in the same sentence, so it means keeping him apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To segregate someone is to separate them from the group, the contrast Beerbohm draws with releasing him among his peers.

clue.text: What he says on entering the Whitehall Banqueting House?

definitions.text: What he says on entering the Whitehall Banqueting House?

blocks.note: surface reading: the words some visitor says as he walks in
setter's reading: the man who says them is the building's architect, and his remark is also his first name

explanation.walkthrough: Inigo Jones designed the Banqueting House in Whitehall, London; walking in he might say 'In I go', which runs together as his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The architect Inigo Jones designed the Banqueting House, completed in 1622, so his first name fits the man entering it.

clue.text: Go underground perhaps in experimental equipment

blocks.note: to have a go at something is to try or test it
the Tube is the London Underground railway

explanation.surface: A suggestion to go into hiding inside some laboratory apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go underground' reads as hiding, but the words split: a go is a trial, and the Tube is London's underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A test tube is a thin glass vessel used to hold samples during laboratory experiments.

clue.text: Month in which he ends in being 14 of 20

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the closing letter of the pronoun is kept

blocks.note: the eighth month of the year
taken as written
the last letter of he

explanation.surface: Someone finishes up in a particular summer month as a holder of high office.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 of 20 means ARCHBISHOP of CANTERBURY: Augustine of Canterbury was the first, sent to England in 597 (a different man from Augustine of Hippo, though both share the name).
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Augustine of Canterbury was the first holder of the office of Archbishop of Canterbury, so he is one of its archbishops.

clue.text: Giovanni Signorini painted it on artist's return

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
RA, Royal Academician, is an artist

explanation.surface: An Italian painter's subject, painted after the artist came back.
explanation.walkthrough: Read ON plus RA backwards to get ARNO. RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Signorini, a nineteenth-century Florentine painter, is known for views of the river that flows through Florence.

clue.text: "His — is from the end of the heaven" (Psalms)

definitions.text: "His — is from the end of the heaven" (Psalms)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line from the Book of Psalms
setter's reading: the dash is a blank for the sun's setting out, as the King James Bible words it

explanation.walkthrough: Psalm 19:6 in the King James Version: 'His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it', describing the sun's daily course.
explanation.definitionFit: The verse describes the sun's emergence each morning, its setting out across the sky from one horizon.

clue.text: Was going to school to acquire neutral vowel sounds

blocks.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone used to attend lessons to pick up the indistinct 'uh' sound in speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to' only places the second word after the first, the school abbreviation, with no shuffling; 'Was' reads like a past tense but is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa is the unstressed, neutral vowel heard at the start of 'about', so schwas are such vowel sounds.

clue.text: I'm put out about short BBC concert that's unprepared

indicators.note: put out can mean disordered, so the verb's letters are knocked out of order
about means surrounding, so the outer words go round the concert

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged
prom is short for promenade concert, as in the BBC Proms

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed about a brief concert on the BBC that is thrown together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm put out' reads as annoyance, but 'out' works on the verb alone. The Proms are the BBC's annual summer season of concerts in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Impromptu describes something done on the spur of the moment, without rehearsal or planning.

clue.text: Sounds like you'll see them in the river at Oxford

definitions.text: Sounds like you'll see them in the river at Oxford

indicators.note: sounds like means the answer is said the same as the word described, though spelt differently

blocks.clueFragment: you'll see them in the river at Oxford
blocks.note: Eights Week is Oxford's summer rowing regatta, where eight-oared boats race on the river

explanation.surface: Something whose name echoes what you'd spot on the Thames at Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings work: eights, the rowing boats, are seen on the river at Oxford, and so are eyots, little islands, pronounced the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyot is a small island in a river, especially the Thames, so such islets are indeed seen there.

clue.text: What could be represented as sliding?

definitions.text: What could be represented as sliding?

indicators.note: to represent letters is to present them again in a fresh form, so the words that follow are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what sort of thing might be shown as a slide.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a glissando is a musical slide, and the letters of the last two words rearrange into its plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Glissandi are musical slides from one pitch to another, written in a score as a line between notes.

clue.text: Work hard without being sanctimonious, returning where 1 4 came from

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the first pair of words wraps round the word for sanctimonious
something returning goes back the way it came, so the whole string is read from right to left

blocks.note: op, short for opus, is a work
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
pi is the informal word for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A plea to labour diligently without getting smug, coming back to the saint's birthplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is used in its old sense of outside. 1 4 is SAINT AUGUSTINE, Bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustine is known as Augustine of Hippo, the Roman North African city where he served as bishop.

clue.text: Initiates in Eleusinian mysteries engaged in overthrowing last popes

indicators.note: something engaged in a thing is caught up inside it, so the letters are found within the words that follow
to overthrow is to turn upside down, which in a clue means reading the letters backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Ancient Greek initiates took part in deposing the most recent pontiffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters STPOPE straddle 'last popes'; read backwards they give EPOPTS.
explanation.definitionFit: An epopt was one admitted to the highest grade of the Eleusinian mysteries, the secret rites of Demeter at Eleusis.

clue.text: Origen Adamantius heartlessly chastised old duffers

indicators.note: without a heart the inside of the name is removed, leaving only its two outer letters
a chastised thing has been beaten and knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters of Adamantius

explanation.surface: The early Church Father Origen, also called Adamantius, harshly rebuked some elderly fools.
explanation.walkthrough: Origen Adamantius was a third-century Christian theologian, a fitting name in a puzzle about Augustine. IGNARO is an archaic word, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignaro is an archaic term for an ignorant person or dunce, which is what a duffer is.

clue.text: Old people suffering set back after PM loses the head

indicators.note: losing the head means dropping the first letter of the name
set back means the word is put back to front, read from right to left

blocks.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a Victorian British Prime Minister
taken as written

explanation.surface: Elderly folk in distress have been set back by a Prime Minister being ousted.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli without his D, followed by SET reversed. 'Suffering' belongs to the definition, recalling the Israelites' bondage in Egypt; it is not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israelites, the ancient Hebrew nation of the Old Testament, suffered slavery in Egypt before the Exodus.

clue.text: Cunning man, like Guareschi's Don Candido

blocks.note: arch means sly or knowing
a bishop is one of the men, or pieces, in chess

explanation.surface: A crafty fellow resembling a clerical character from the Italian writer Guareschi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' reads as a person, but it is a chessman. Giovannino Guareschi was the Italian author of the Don Camillo stories about a village priest and his superiors.
explanation.definitionFit: Guareschi's Don Candido is a churchman of senior rank, an archbishop being a bishop who heads a province of the church.

clue.text: Broadcast second coming about first part of festival, as 1 4 did

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered far and wide, so the letters are scattered and rearranged
coming about means going around, so the rearranged word surrounds the festival's opening

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening three letters of festival

explanation.surface: Announcing the Second Coming near the start of a religious feast, just as the saint did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second coming' reads as one phrase but splits apart. 1 4 is SAINT AUGUSTINE, author of the Confessions.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustine's Confessions is his autobiography admitting his sins, so he owned up to them in writing.

clue.text: Unwanted correspondence of priest replacing Catholic in deception

indicators.note: one thing replacing another takes its place, so one letter is swapped out for another inside the word

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for priest
C is the abbreviation for Catholic
a scam is a swindle or deception

explanation.surface: Letters a cleric would rather not get, about a priest standing in for a Catholic in a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: In SCAM, the C for Catholic gives way to P for priest, making SPAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is junk email, the bulk messages that nobody asked to receive.

clue.text: On which Pilgrim's Progress was obtained?

definitions.text: On which Pilgrim's Progress was obtained?

blocks.note: surface reading: a copy of Bunyan's book, acquired somewhere

blocks.clueFragment: On which Pilgrim's Progress was obtained?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the ship on which the Pilgrim Fathers made their voyage to America in 1620

explanation.walkthrough: A twin of 20 across: the progress of pilgrims, this time the Pilgrim Fathers crossing the Atlantic, made on board a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mayflower carried the Pilgrim Fathers from Plymouth to New England in 1620, the vessel their journey was made on.

clue.text: Entering University Dr Freud's instinct is to master religious doctrine

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the letter for university is placed within the following words

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written
in Freudian theory the id is the seat of instinctive drives
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for master, as in an MA

explanation.surface: Joining a university, Dr Freud instinctively wants to get on top of a faith's teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The university letter goes inside the doctor and the instinct together, not inside the doctor alone; the druids were the priests of ancient Celtic Britain and Gaul.
explanation.definitionFit: Druidism is the religion of the ancient Celtic priests called druids, a system of belief and teaching.

clue.text: Time spent in shrine on supplication

indicators.note: time spent in a place is held within it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Hours passed in a holy place, given over to prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eons are immensely long periods, so the word stands for time in the sense of ages.

clue.text: Where Pilgrim's Progress ended up?

blocks.note: surface reading: Bunyan's allegory The Pilgrim's Progress
setter's reading: the destination reached by the pilgrims travelling together in Chaucer's tales

explanation.walkthrough: Bunyan's book makes you think of the Celestial City, but read as plain words it is the progress of pilgrims, and Chaucer's pilgrims were heading for a cathedral city in Kent; 4 across was its first archbishop.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales follows pilgrims riding to the shrine of Thomas Becket in the cathedral city, their journey's end.

clue.text: Purify while ingesting it

indicators.note: to ingest is to take into the body, so one word swallows the other

blocks.note: when and while both mean at the time that
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cleanse something even as you swallow it.
explanation.definitionFit: To whiten can mean to make pure or spotless, cleansing of stain as well as of colour.

clue.text: Liberal grasp on what The Man of Property has

definitions.text: what The Man of Property has

blocks.note: free as in generous or liberal
a hold is a grip or grasp

explanation.surface: A generous grip on whatever Galsworthy's propertied hero owns.
explanation.walkthrough: The Man of Property is the first novel of Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga, about the acquisitive Soames Forsyte; 'Liberal' with a capital letter suggests the party, but it is just generous.
explanation.definitionFit: Freehold is outright ownership of land or buildings, exactly what a man of property possesses.

clue.text: One of the things 1 4 wrote about it in a note

definitions.text: One of the things 1 4 wrote about

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the pronoun sits within the musical note

blocks.note: fah is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale
taken as written

explanation.surface: A subject the saint wrote on, put into a short memo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' reads as a written memo but is the sol-fa syllable. 1 4 is SAINT AUGUSTINE, whose writings include a handbook on faith, hope and charity.
explanation.definitionFit: Faith, religious belief and trust in God, is a central theme of Augustine's theology, including his Enchiridion.

clue.text: Dante's guide watching while crossing river

indicators.note: crossing a thing means stretching across it on either side, so one word straddles the other

blocks.note: a vigil is a period of keeping watch
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: The poet who led Dante through the underworld keeps an eye out while he crosses a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet Virgil leads Dante through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy.

clue.text: Information about them is obtained from headings in Hervarar Saga

definitions.text: Information about them is obtained from headings in Hervarar Saga

indicators.note: the heading of a word is what stands at its head, so only the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: got means obtained
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A reader learns about a people from the chapter titles of an Old Norse saga.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: the Hervarar Saga tells of wars between the Goths and the Huns.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Norse Hervarar saga preserves legends of the Goths, the Germanic people of late antiquity.

clue.text: Manages with difficulty to make some earnings with a Ken Loach movie

indicators.note: some means just a little of the word, here its first letter only

blocks.note: the first letter of earnings
Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel

explanation.surface: A film-maker scrapes by, earning a little from one of Ken Loach's films.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out a living is to scrape by, getting just enough through effort and thrift.

clue.text: Some picture featuring Spielberg's lead in fashionable movie of his

indicators.note: the lead of a name is the letter in front, so only the director's initial is used
a film featuring an actor has them inside it, so the initial goes within the following words

blocks.note: the first letter of Spielberg
in means fashionable
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is Spielberg's 1982 film

explanation.surface: Part of a film image showing Spielberg's star in one of his trendy movies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' looks like a film after all the movie talk, but here it is an image.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small illustration set within a larger picture or page, so it forms part of the whole.

clue.text: Deceive two about to be accompanied by …

indicators.note: about can mean in a jumbled, scattered fashion, so the number's letters are turned around in order

blocks.note: to take someone in is to fool them
the number written out

explanation.surface: Fool a couple who are about to be escorted by the people in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs this clue into 28 across: someone takes pleasure seekers in tow.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone in tow is to have them follow along with you, so they are accompanied by you.

clue.text: … pleasure seekers including Quixote in robberies

indicators.note: including something means holding it inside, so the knight's title goes inside the word for robberies

blocks.note: heists are robberies
Cervantes' hero is Don Quixote, so his title stands in

explanation.surface: Thrill-seekers who drag Don Quixote along on their raids.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedonists live for pleasure, so they are people seeking enjoyment above all else.

clue.text: I'm cheeseparing Parmesan I grated without a pan perhaps

definitions.note: the answer speaks: the clue means 'I'm a cheeseparing type', a noun

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away from the fodder
grated cheese is shredded into bits, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written
these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A stingy cook grates Parmesan straight onto the counter to save using a pan.
explanation.walkthrough: Take A, P, A and N from PARMESAN I, leaving RMESI to rearrange. The whole clue also describes the miserly speaker, which is why 'perhaps' closes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheeseparing means meanly economical, the defining habit of a miser who hoards every penny.
